entries.37b70ae54c7cf9e8e34756a3bcfd95d52803eebc: 1Ki 17:7-9 <div eID="gen5012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5013" type="x-p"/> After some time this brook dried up for want of rain. Then the Lord directed His servant to go to the Sidonian <hi type="italic">Zarephath</hi>, and to live with a widow whom He had commanded to provide for him. ימים מקּץ does not mean <hi type="italic">post annum</hi>, for ימים merely derives this meaning in certain passages from the context (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.29">Lev 25:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.7">1Sa 27:7</reference>; Jdg 17:10); whereas in this instance the context does not point to the space of a year, but to a longer period of indefinite duration, all that we know being that, according to 1Ki 18:1, the sojourn of Elijah at Cherith and Zarephath lasted at least two years. Zarephath (Σαρέπτα, lxx) was situated on the Mediterranean Sea between Tyre and Sidon, where a miserable Mohammedan village with ruins and a promontory, <hi type="italic">Surafend</hi>, still preserve the name of the former town (Rob. iii. p. 413ff., and V. de Velde, <hi type="italic">Syria and Palestine</hi>, i. pp. 101-3, transl.).
entries.5a191e74850323c309127ac4ea2ba82d800f7a31: 1Ki 17:10-12 <div eID="gen5013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5014" type="x-p"/> When Elijah arrived at the city gate, he met a widow engaged in gathering wood. To discover whether it was to her that the Lord had sent him, he asked her for something to drink and for a morsel of bread to eat; whereupon she assured him, with an oath by Jehovah, that she had nothing baked (מעוג = עגּה, ἐγκρυφίας, a cake baked in hot ashes), but only a handful of meal in the כּד (a pail or small vessel in which meal was kept) and a little oil in the pitcher, and that she was just gathering wood to dress this remnant for herself and her son, that they might eat it, and then die. From this statement of the widow it is evident, on the one hand, that the drought and famine had spread across the Phoenician frontier, as indeed Menander of Ephesus attests;<note placement="foot">Josephus gives this statement from his Phoenician history: ἀβροχία τε ἐπ ̓ αὐτοῦ (sc., Ἰθοβάλου) ἐγένετο ἀπὸ τοῦ Ὑπερβερεταίου μηνὸς ἕως τοῦ ἐρχομένου ἔτους Ὑπερβερεταίου (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. viii. 13, 2). <hi type="italic">Hyperberetaeus</hi> answers to <hi type="italic">Tishri</hi> of the Hebrews; cf. Benfey and Stern, <hi type="italic">die Monatsnamen</hi>, p. 18.</note> on the other hand, the widow showed by the oath, “as Jehovah thy God liveth,” that she was a worshipper of the true God, who spoke of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> as his God, because she recognised the prophet as an Israelite.
entries.07209c4410ae833e8f9af975baaf33a7d24464f2: 1Ki 17:13-16 <div eID="gen5014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5015" type="x-p"/> In order, however, to determine with indisputable certainty whether this believing Gentile was the protectress assigned him by the Lord, Elijah comforted her, and at the same time desired her first of all to bake him a little cake משּׁם, i.e., of the last of the meal in the <hi type="italic">Kad</hi> and of the oil in the pitcher, and then to bake for herself and her son, adding this promise: Jehovah the God of Israel will not let the meal in the <hi type="italic">Kad</hi> and the oil in the pitcher fail, till He sends rain upon the earth again. And the widow did according to his word. She gave up the certain for the uncertain, because she trusted the word of the Lord, and received the reward of her believing confidence in the fact that during the whole time of the drought she suffered from no want of either meal or oil. This act of the pious Gentile woman, who had welcomed with a simple heart the knowledge of the true God that had reached her from Israel, must have been the source of strong consolation to Elijah in the hour of conflict, when his faith was trembling because of the multitude of idolaters in Israel. If the Lord Himself had raised up true worshipers of His name among the Gentiles, his work in Israel could not be put to shame. <div eID="gen5015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5016" type="x-p"/> The believing widow, however, received from the prophet not only a material blessing, but a spiritual blessing also. For, as Christ tells His unbelieving contemporaries to their shame (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.25-Luke.4.26">Luk 4:25-26</reference>), Elijah was not sent to this widow in order that he might be safely hidden at her house, although this object was better attained thereby than by his remaining longer in Israel; but because of her faith, namely, to strengthen and to increase it, he was sent to her, and not to one of the many widows in Israel, many of whom would also have received the prophet if they had been rescued by him from the pressure of the famine. And the miraculous increase of the meal and oil did not merely subserve the purpose of keeping the prophet and the widow alive; but the relief of her bodily need was also meant to be a preparatory means of quieting her spiritual need as well. On the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> תתּן, see at 1Ki 6:19. In 1Ki 17:15 the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> והוּה היא is an unnecessary emendation of the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> והיא הוּא; the feminine form ותּאכל is occasioned primarily by the preceding verbs, and may be taken as an indefinite neuter: “and there ate he and she.” The offence which Thenius has taken at ימים (days) has no foundation, if we do not understand the sentence as referring merely to their eating once of the bread just baked, but take it generally as signifying that in consequence of their acting according to the word of Jehovah, they (Elijah, the widow, and her family) ate for days, i.e., until God sent rain again (1Ki 17:14).
entries.012443e88f0d370aae96d129a349e7a9735a7822: 1Ki 17:17 <hi type="italic">The widow’s deceased son raised to life again</hi>. - 1Ki 17:17. After these events, when Elijah had taken up his abode in the upper room of her house, her son fell sick, so that he breathed out his life. וגו אשׁר עד, literally till no breath remained in him. That these words do not signify merely a death-like torpor, but an actual decease, is evident from what follows, where Elijah himself treats the boy as dead, and the Lord, in answer to his prayer, restores him to life again.
entries.9f2e807574ca956e06aed72283a9163465abbc9f: 1Ki 17:18 <div eID="gen5016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5017" type="x-p"/> The pious woman discerned in this death a punishment from God for her sin, and supposed that it had been drawn towards her by the presence of the man of God, so that she said to Elijah, “What have we to do with one another (מה־לּי ולך; cf. Jdg 11:12; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">2Sa 16:10</reference>), thou man of God? Hast thou come to me to bring my sin to remembrance (with God), and to kill my son?” In this half-heathenish belief there spoke at the same time a mind susceptible to divine truth and conscious of its sin, to which the Lord could not refuse His aid. Like the blindness in the case of the man born blind mentioned in John 9, the death of this widow’s son was not sent as a punishment for particular sins, but was intended as a medium for the manifestation of the works of God in her (Joh 9:3), in order that she might learn that the Lord was not merely the God of the Jews, but the God of the Gentiles also (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.29">Rom 3:29</reference>).
entries.b6f009d10630ece351c550458fd5980a34f429af: 1Ki 17:19-20 <div eID="gen5017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5018" type="x-p"/> Elijah told her to carry the dead child up to the chamber in which he lived and lay it upon his bed, and then cried to the Lord, “Jehovah, my God! hast Thou also brought evil upon the widow with whom I sojourn, to slay her son?” These words, in which the word <hi type="italic">also</hi> refers to the other calamities occasioned by the drought, contain no reproach of God, but are expressive of the heartiest compassion for the suffering of his benefactress and the deepest lamentation, which, springing from living faith, pours out the whole heart before God in the hour of distress, that I may appeal to Him the more powerfully for His aid. The meaning is, “Thou, O Lord my God, according to Thy grace and righteousness, canst not possibly leave the son of this widow in death.” Such confident belief carries within itself the certainty of being heard. The prophet therefore proceeds at once to action, to restore the boy to life.
entries.68151a6fbac81e369f35a528837674e028ae1799: 1Ki 17:21 <div eID="gen5018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5019" type="x-p"/> He stretched himself (יתמדד) three times upon him, not to ascertain whether there was still any life left in him, as Paul did in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.10">Act 20:10</reference>, nor to warm the body of the child and set its blood in circulation, as Elisha did with a dead child (2Ki 4:34), - for the action of Elisha is described in a different manner, and the youth mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.10">Act 20:10</reference> was only apparently dead, - but to bring down the vivifying power of God upon the dead body, and thereby support his own word and prayer.<note placement="foot">“This was done, that the prophet’s body might be the instrument of the miracle, just as in other cases of miracle there was an imposition of the hand.” - Seb. Schmidt.</note> <div eID="gen5019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5020" type="x-p"/> He then cried to the Lord, “Jehovah, my God, I pray Thee let the soul of this boy return within it.” על־קרבּו, inasmuch as the soul as the vital principle springs from above.
entries.bf68a068d346a8a28d18f6ca89f0abe90feb4cd3: 1Ki 17:22-23 <div eID="gen5020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5021" type="x-p"/> The Lord heard this prayer: the boy came to life again; whereupon Elijah gave him back to his mother.
entries.635629819dc6890e9f3d723246246097df65ea08: 1Ki 17:24 <div eID="gen5021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5022" type="x-p"/> Through this miracle, in which Elijah showed himself as the forerunner of Him who raiseth all the dead to life, the pious Gentile woman was mightily strengthened in her faith in the God of Israel. She now not only recognised Elijah as a man of God, as in 1Ki 17:18, but perceived that the word of Jehovah in his mouth was truth, by which she confessed <hi type="italic">implicite</hi> her faith in the God of Israel as the true God. As the judgment of drought and famine did not bring king Ahab to his senses and lead him to turn from his ungodly ways, but only filled him with exasperation towards the prophet who had announced to him the coming judgment; there was no other course left than to lay before the people with mighty and convincing force the proof that Jehovah was the only true God, and to execute judgment upon the priests of Baal as the seducers of the nation.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.17"/> <div eID="gen5022" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> the barrel of meal wasted not <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">God still Creating new, as fast as the old was spent.</ns0:note>, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> by the hand of.</ns0:note> by Elijah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 ¶ And it came to pass after these things, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick, and his sickness was so sore, that there was no breath <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>no Soul,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Life,</ns0:hi> as this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Word oft signifies: <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He died, as is manifest from the following Verses. See also <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11. 35.</ns0:note> left in him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And she said unto Elijah, What have I to do with thee <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Wherein have I injured or provoked thee? Or, Why didst thou come to Sojourn in my House, (as the following Words seem to Explain these) if this be the fruit of it? They are Words of a troubled Mind, favouring of some rashness and impatience.</ns0:note>, O thou man of God? art thou come unto me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Didst thou come for this end, that thou mightest severely observe my Sins, and by thy prayers bring down God's just Judgment upon me, for them, as thou hast for the like cause brought down this Famine upon the Nation?</ns0:note> to call my sin to remembrance <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either, 1. To my remembrance; that I should by this dreadful Judgment be brought to the knowledge and remembrance of my Sins, which have pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cured it. Or rather, 2. To God's Remembrance: for God is oft said in Scripture, to <ns0:hi>remember sins,</ns0:hi> when he punisheth them; and to <ns0:hi>forget</ns0:hi> them, when he spares the Sinner. See 2 <ns0:hi>Sem.</ns0:hi> 16. 10. Have I instead of the Blessing which I ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pected from thy presence, met with a Curse?</ns0:note>, and to stay my son?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And he said unto her, Give me thy son <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Into mine Arms.</ns0:note>. And he took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into a loft <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">A private place, where he might more freely and fully pour out his Soul to God, and use such Gestures or Methods, as he thought most proper, with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out any offence or observation.</ns0:note>, where he abode, and laid him upon his own bed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And he cried unto the LORD, and said, O LORD my God, hast thou also brought evil upon the widow, with whom I sojourn, by slay<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing her son <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">A Prayer full of powerful Arguments. Thou art <ns0:hi>the Lord,</ns0:hi> that canst revive the Child: and <ns0:hi>my God;</ns0:hi> and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore wiltst not, do not deny me. She is <ns0:hi>a widow,</ns0:hi> add not Affliction to the Afflicted; deprive her not of the great support and staff of her Age; She hath given me kind en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tertainment: let her not fare the worse for her kindness to a Prophet, whereby Wicked Men will take occasion to Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proach both her, and Religion.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And he <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sured.</ns0:note> stretched himself upon the child <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not as if he thought this could contribute any warmth or Life to the Child; but partly, to express, and withal to increase his grief for the Child's Death, and his desire of its reviving; that thereby his Prayers might be more fervent, and consequently, more prevalent with God: and partly, that it might appear, That this Miracle, though wrought by God alone, yet was done for the sake of <ns0:hi>Elijah,</ns0:hi> and in answer to his Prayers. Compare 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 4. 34. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 20. 10.</ns0:note> three times, and cried unto the LORD <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">First, he stretched himself, then he prayed, and that for Three times successively.</ns0:note>, and said, O LORD my God, I pray thee let this childs soul come <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> into <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> inward parts.</ns0:note> into him again <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By which it is evident, That the Soul was gone out of his Body, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore doth subsist without it after Death. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 18. This was a great Request; but <ns0:hi>Elias</ns0:hi> was incouraged to make it; partly, by his Zeal for God's Honour, which he thought was concerned in it, and would be Eclipsed by it: partly, by the experience which he had of his prevailing<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />power with God in prayer: and partly, by a Divine Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pulse moving him to desire it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And the LORD heard the voice of Elijah, and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the chamber into the house, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livered him unto his mother: and Elijah said, See, thy son liveth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ And the woman said to Elijah, Now by this I know <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Now I am assured of that concerning which I began up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on this sad occasion to doubt.</ns0:note> that thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> a man of God, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> the word of the LORD in thy mouth <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> truth <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That the God whom thou professest, is the True God; and the Doctrine and Religion which thou Teachest, is the onely True Religion: and therefore henceforth I wholly Renounce the Worship of Idols.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
